Rule34 Tag Watcher: The Doomsday File
This is the file for Future Me, Curious You, or Whoever Is Staring At A Dead Drive At 2 A.M.
It explains what the watcher does, how to install it from nothing, how the storage trick works, how to recover it, and how to unstick Windows Task Scheduler when it decides to become a cryptid.
The short version: this is a Windows Python downloader for exact Rule34 tags. It checks for new posts on a schedule, can backfill all available history, and uses NTFS hard links so one post can appear in several tag folders without storing several physical copies.
What you need

Windows 10 or 11
Python 3.10 or newer from python.org
An NTFS drive for the archive
A Rule34 account, numeric user ID, and API key
The project files from this repository or the release ZIP
Enough free space for the inevitable consequences of your decisions

The watcher uses only Python’s standard library. You do not need pip.
What the finished archive looks like
Rule34 Tag Archive\
├── Copyright\
│   └── example_series\
├── Character\
│   └── example_character\
├── Artist\
│   └── example_artist\
├── General\
│   └── example_general_tag\
└── .r34-watcher\
    ├── files\
    │   └── ...one canonical copy of every post...
    ├── state.sqlite3
    └── watcher.lock
The visible category files and the canonical file are NTFS hard links. They are multiple names for the same physical bytes.
Do not delete .r34-watcher. It contains the canonical file links and the database that remembers what happened.
The five-minute clean install
1. Install Python
Install Python 3.10 or newer from python.org. During setup, enable the option that adds Python to PATH or installs the py launcher.
Open Command Prompt and confirm:
py -3 --version
If py is unavailable, try:
python --version
2. Get the project
Download the repository as a ZIP and extract it somewhere permanent, or clone it:
git clone github.com/ToastSweat/r34-tag-watcher.git
cd r34-tag-watcher
Do not run the watcher from inside a ZIP. Do not schedule it from a temporary Downloads folder unless you enjoy leaving traps for yourself.
3. Get Rule34 API credentials
Log into Rule34, open the account options page, and generate an API key.
The site may display a fragment resembling:
&api_key=ABC123&user_id=456789
The configuration needs only the values:
"user_id": "456789",
"api_key": "ABC123"
Do not include user_id=, api_key=, &, or the combined URL fragment.
Never commit config.json. It contains the API key in plain text because the unattended task must be able to read it.
4. Run setup
Open PowerShell in the extracted project folder and run:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\setup.ps1
Setup asks for:

Archive destination
Copyright tags
Character tags
Artist tags
General tags
Check interval
Numeric user ID
API key

Enter tags exactly as the site displays them. Use underscores, not spaces. Separate multiple tags with commas.
Setup writes config.json, checks that the archive drive supports hard links, and installs a scheduled task named Rule34 Tag Watcher.
5. Test it visibly
Double-click:
run_now.bat
Or run it from Command Prompt:
run_now.bat
The first normal run downloads the newest 25 posts for each tag by default. Older results in the scanned pages become a baseline so the hourly watcher can concentrate on new posts.
6. Download history if wanted
Double-click:
run_backfill.bat
Backfill walks every available API page for every configured tag. It is safe to interrupt and rerun. Completed work is skipped, baseline entries are revisited, and overlapping posts receive more hard links rather than more downloaded copies.
Popular tags can take a very long time. Leave the one-second request delay alone unless you have a compelling reason to annoy the API.
Manual configuration
If you do not want to use setup, copy config.example.json to config.json and edit it:
{
  "output_directory": "D:\\Rule34 Tag Archive",
  "api": {
    "base_url": "api.rule34.xxx/index.php",
    "user_id": "456789",
    "api_key": "ABC123"
  },
  "watched_tags": {
    "copyright": ["example_series"],
    "character": ["example_character"],
    "artist": ["example_artist"],
    "general": ["example_general_tag"]
  },
  "schedule": {
    "interval_minutes": 60
  },
  "scan": {
    "results_per_page": 100,
    "pages_per_check": 3,
    "first_run_download_limit_per_tag": 25,
    "max_downloads_per_tag_per_run": 100,
    "request_delay_seconds": 1.0,
    "request_timeout_seconds": 45,
    "retry_attempts": 3
  },
  "downloads": {
    "allowed_extensions": [".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp"],
    "save_sidecar_metadata": false
  }
}
Add .mp4 and .webm to allowed_extensions before backfill if videos are wanted too.
Validate the configuration and hard-link support without contacting the site:
py -3 .\r34_tag_watcher.py --config .\config.json --check-config
Preview destinations without downloading:
py -3 .\r34_tag_watcher.py --config .\config.json --dry-run
The deduplication trick
Each post is downloaded into:
.r34-watcher\files\<two-character-shard>\<post-id>_<hash>.<extension>
The watcher then calls the operating system’s hard-link function for every matching tag destination.
That gives us all three properties we wanted:

Every tag folder contains ordinary browsable files.
A post can appear under several tags.
The file data consumes space once.

Useful facts:

Hard links must live on the same filesystem volume.
The archive destination must support them; on Windows that normally means NTFS.
Deleting one tag link does not destroy the bytes while another hard link still exists.
Explorer’s folder Properties may count every path and exaggerate used space.
The drive’s free-space change is the reliable measure of physical storage use.
A normal cross-drive copy usually dereferences the links and creates full duplicates.

Installing, checking, and removing the scheduled task
Install or reinstall it from Command Prompt or PowerShell:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install_task.ps1
Verify it from Command Prompt:
schtasks /Query /TN "Rule34 Tag Watcher" /V /FO LIST
Verify it from PowerShell:
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher"
Get-ScheduledTask is a PowerShell command. Command Prompt will say it is not recognized if you paste it there without launching PowerShell. That does not mean the task is broken.
Remove only the task:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\uninstall_task.ps1
Removing the task does not delete the archive, configuration, database, or logs.
Moving the project or archive
There are two different things:

The project folder contains the Python and launcher scripts.
The archive folder contains the media, hard links, and SQLite state.

If the project folder moves, the scheduled task still points at the old absolute path. Changing config.json is not enough. Remove the old task before the move and reinstall it from the new project folder afterward.
Safe project-folder move:

Run uninstall_task.ps1 from the old project folder.
Move the project folder.
Update output_directory only if the archive also moved.
Run install_task.ps1 from the new project folder.
Run run_now.bat once and check the log.

Moving the archive to another drive is more delicate. A normal Explorer copy can turn every hard link into a separate physical file. Until a dedicated migration tool exists, the safest space-efficient choices are:

Start a fresh archive on the new NTFS drive and run backfill again, or
Use a proven hard-link-aware backup/migration tool and verify the result before deleting the source.

Never delete the source archive until the destination has been verified. Check matching files with:
fsutil hardlink list "D:\Rule34 Tag Archive\Character\some_tag\some_file.jpg"
The output should include both the visible tag path and a path under .r34-watcher\files on the same volume.
Fixing “Another watcher run is already in progress”
The watcher creates:
<archive>\.r34-watcher\watcher.lock
That stops the scheduled check and a manual backfill from modifying the database at the same time.
First, see whether the scheduled task is actually running:
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher" | Select-Object TaskName, State
If it says Running, let it finish. A backfill may genuinely take hours.
If it is stuck and you intentionally want to stop it:
Disable-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher"
Stop-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='python.exe' OR Name='pythonw.exe' OR Name='py.exe'" |
  Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -like '*r34_tag_watcher.py*' } |
  ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force }
Only after confirming no watcher Python process remains, remove the stale lock. Replace the path with the real archive path:
Remove-Item "D:\Rule34 Tag Archive\.r34-watcher\watcher.lock" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Run run_now.bat. If it succeeds, re-enable the task:
Enable-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Rule34 Tag Watcher"
Do not casually delete the lock while a watcher is alive. Two concurrent writers are exactly what the lock is preventing.
Common failures
Missing authentication
Both credentials are required. Confirm user_id contains numbers only and api_key contains only the key value.
Unexpected API response type
Old builds hid string messages from the API. Current builds unwrap double-encoded JSON, treat “No images found” as an empty result, and display real API messages while redacting the configured API key.
Nothing downloads on the second normal run
That is usually correct. The first run establishes a baseline; later normal runs only download new discoveries. Use backfill for history.
The task exists but does not run after reboot
The task uses an interactive-logon principal. It runs while the configured Windows account is logged in. Check its action path with schtasks; if the project moved, reinstall the task.
The archive appears several times larger than the drive space used
Explorer is adding the logical size of every hard-link path. Check actual drive free space and verify links with fsutil hardlink list.
A tag file was deleted
The watcher repairs a missing managed link the next time that post is encountered. It does not redownload the bytes if the canonical file still exists.
Recovery scenarios
The project folder vanished, but the archive survived

Download the project again.
Create a new config.json pointing at the existing archive.
Use the same watched tags.
Run --check-config.
Run run_now.bat.
Reinstall the scheduled task.

The history database lives in the archive, so it should be found automatically.
The database vanished, but .r34-watcher\files survived
Make a backup first. Then run backfill. The watcher can recognize existing canonical files, rebuild records, and restore missing tag links without downloading those bytes again.
Everything vanished
Install from the repository, restore the tag lists and credentials, choose a new NTFS archive, test normally, and run backfill.
This is why the safe-to-share parts belong on GitHub and the secret config.json does not.
Running the test suite
From the project folder:
py -3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
The tests cover configuration validation, API response oddities, initial baselining, new-post checks, resumable multi-page backfill, General tags, one-download/multiple-link behavior, and link repair.
Reimplementing it from the design
If the source somehow disappears from every backup, these are the essential pieces:

Load and validate JSON configuration.
Represent every watched item as a category/tag pair.
Query the Rule34 DAPI with page=dapi, s=post, q=index, json=1, tags, pid, limit, user_id, and api_key.
Normalize normal lists, message strings, and double-encoded JSON responses.
Rate-limit and retry all requests.
Store tag initialization, per-tag post status, and canonical file paths in SQLite.
Download into a temporary .part file, verify it is non-empty, then atomically move it into the canonical store.
Use post ID plus file hash for collision-resistant filenames.
Use os.link to create every visible tag path from the canonical file.
Refuse to replace unrelated existing files.
Use a single-instance lock around database and archive changes.
Keep normal checks bounded; make full backfill explicit and resumable.
Log to both the console and rotating files.
Schedule only normal mode. Backfill remains a deliberate manual operation.

That is the whole machine.
One polite API client.
One memory.
One physical copy of every file.
As many useful folder paths as you want.
Good luck, Future Me.

Shag’s Lab: The Doomsday Rebuild Guide
This is the file for Future Me, Curious You, or Whoever Is Looking At A Dead PC Wondering Why A Personal Wiki Needed A Build Pipeline.
The short version:
The Obsidian vault is the source of truth.
Everything else is replaceable.
The live site is a static Quartz build made from explicitly public notes in that vault. The vault and generated site live in one private Git repository. The home PC builds and pushes it. The web host pulls it and copies only the finished public files into Apache’s web root.
If every piece of software involved in this project vanished tomorrow, the important part would still be a folder full of Markdown files and images.
That is the point.
Current layout
Home PC
F:\[DIARY]\
├── Shag's Lab\                 <-- SOURCE OF TRUTH / Git repository
│   ├── .git\
│   ├── .obsidian\
│   ├── Projects\
│   ├── Updates\
│   ├── Welcome.md
│   └── .site\
│       └── public\             <-- generated static website, committed to Git
│
└── ShagsLab-Web\               <-- disposable Quartz/build machinery
    ├── content\                <-- regenerated staging content
    ├── public\                 <-- Quartz build output
    ├── Publish-Lab.ps1
    └── Quartz files...
GitHub
One private repository:
github.com/ToastSweat/shags-lab
It contains the vault and .site/public.
Keep it private because the repo contains the complete vault, not merely the public website.
Web host
C:\PGN\ShagsLab\                <-- private Git checkout
└── .site\public\               <-- finished site from home PC
 
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab\    <-- Apache PUBLIC directory
Public URL:
helvete.pizza/lab/
Apache serves only:
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab
The full Git checkout is intentionally kept outside htdocs.
The content model
Do not overcomplicate this.
There are two main things:

Updates are chronological diary entries.
Projects are persistent wiki-ish things.

An Update should normally have:
---
type: update
date: 2026-09-19
project: Exact Project Name
publish: true
---
A Project Home should normally have:
---
type: project
project: Exact Project Name
status: active
publish: true
---
The project: value on the Project Home and its Updates should match.
That is how the publisher knows which Updates belong to which Project and can sort Projects by recent activity.
The homepage should contain:
---
title: Welcome
publish: true
---
Updates/Updates Home.md and Projects/Projects Home.md are generated by the publisher.
Do not lovingly hand-maintain those lists. The script will overwrite them.
Anything without:
publish: true
stays out of the public build.
Normal publishing workflow
On the home PC:

Work normally in Obsidian.
Add/update notes.
Set publish: true only on things that should be public.
Run Publish-ShagsLab-HomePC.bat.

That BAT runs the PowerShell publisher.
The publisher:

Scans the vault.
Generates Updates Home.
Generates Projects Home.
Creates a clean Quartz staging directory.
Copies only published notes.
Copies assets referenced by published notes.
Turns Welcome.md into index.md.
Builds Quartz.
Mirrors the built static site into .site\public inside the vault repository.
Commits the vault and generated site.
Pushes main to GitHub.

Then, on the web host, run:
Update-ShagsLab-WebHost.bat
That:

Pulls origin/main.
Verifies .site\public\index.html exists.
Mirrors .site\public into C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab.

Done.
Rebuilding the home PC from GitHub
If the home PC dies but GitHub survives:
1. Install the basics
Install:

Git
Node.js 22 or newer
npm
Obsidian

The setup was originally built with:
Node 24.14.1
npm 11.11.0
Git 2.53.0.windows.2
Quartz 5
Newer compatible versions are fine, but if Future Quartz has changed beyond recognition, use a compatible Quartz v5 release.
2. Recreate the diary directory
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "F:\[DIARY]" -Force
Clone the private repo:
git clone github.com/ToastSweat/shags-lab.git "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
Because [DIARY] contains square brackets, use PowerShell’s literal-path commands when navigating:
Set-Location -LiteralPath "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
Do not rely on:
cd "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
PowerShell may interpret the brackets as a wildcard pattern.
Open F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab as an Obsidian vault.
3. Recreate Quartz
Clone Quartz beside the vault:
git clone github.com/jackyzha0/quartz.git "F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web"
Set-Location -LiteralPath "F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web"
npm i
Initialize it for Obsidian:
npx quartz create --template obsidian --strategy new --baseUrl helvete.pizza/lab
If Quartz complains that the default theme exists but cannot be loaded:
Cannot find module '@quartz-themes/default'
install it explicitly:
npm install @quartz-themes/default
In quartz.config.yaml, make sure the important values are:
configuration:
  pageTitle: "Shag's Lab"
  baseUrl: "helvete.pizza/lab"
The custom publisher performs the public/private filtering before Quartz sees the notes, so the Quartz explicit-publish plugin does not need to be enabled.
Restore Publish-Lab.ps1 from the copy embedded later in this guide.
Save it as:
F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web\Publish-Lab.ps1
Restore the home-PC BAT from this guide as well.
Creating the Git repository from a surviving local vault
If GitHub is gone but the local vault survives:
Set-Location -LiteralPath "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
 
git init
git branch -M main
Use this .gitignore:
.obsidian/workspace.json
.obsidian/workspace-mobile.json
.trash/
Thumbs.db
.DS_Store
desktop.ini
Do not ignore the whole .obsidian directory. The lightweight Obsidian configuration is useful when rebuilding the vault.
Then:
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Shag's Lab vault"
Create a new empty private GitHub repository and connect it:
git remote add origin github.com/ToastSweat/shags-lab.git
git push -u origin main
Rebuilding the web host
The web host does not build Quartz.
It only pulls the one private repo and copies the already-generated website into Apache’s public directory.
Install Git if necessary.
Create the non-public checkout location:
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "C:\PGN" -Force
Clone:
git clone github.com/ToastSweat/shags-lab.git "C:\PGN\ShagsLab"
GitHub authentication may open a browser because the repository is private.
Verify the generated site came down:
Test-Path -LiteralPath "C:\PGN\ShagsLab\.site\public\index.html"
Expected:
True
Restore Update-ShagsLab-WebHost.bat from the copy later in this guide and run it.
It will create this directory if needed:
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab
and mirror the finished site into it.
Important warning about /MIR
The web-host BAT uses:
robocopy ... /MIR
That is intentional.
It makes the Apache directory exactly match the generated site and removes stale files.
Therefore:
Do not store unrelated hand-written files inside C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab.
They may be deleted on the next update.
Testing the pipeline
Home PC
After publishing:
Test-Path -LiteralPath "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab\.site\public\index.html"
Expected:
True
Check Git:
Set-Location -LiteralPath "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
git status
git remote -v
After a successful publisher run, the working tree should normally be clean and origin should point at the private GitHub repo.
Web host
After running the updater:
Test-Path -LiteralPath "C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab\index.html"
Expected:
True
Local Apache test:
http://localhost/lab/
Public test:
helvete.pizza/lab/
Apache and HTTPS
The site is a subdirectory of the existing helvete.pizza Apache site.
Live directory:
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab
The current certificate files for helvete.pizza are:
C:\xampp\apache\certs\helvete.pizza-crt.pem
C:\xampp\apache\certs\helvete.pizza-key.pem
C:\xampp\apache\certs\helvete.pizza-chain.pem
The Apache SSL configuration is in:
C:\xampp\apache\conf\extra\httpd-ssl.conf
Before restarting Apache after certificate/configuration changes:
C:\xampp\apache\bin\httpd.exe -t
Expected:
Syntax OK
Then restart Apache from the XAMPP Control Panel.
Reissuing the helvete.pizza certificate with win-acme
Run wacs.exe as Administrator.
The working manual setup used:

M - Create certificate (full options)
Manually input host name:
helvete.pizza

4 - Single certificate
1 - HTTP: save verification files on a path
Root path:
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete

Do not copy the default web.config
2 - RSA key
2 - PEM encoded files
PEM destination:
C:\xampp\apache\certs

1 - No password on the private-key PEM
5 - No additional storage steps
3 - No additional installation steps

Successful output included:
Authorization result: valid
Exporting .pem files to C:\xampp\apache\certs
Scheduled task looks healthy
Certificate helvete.pizza created
Then validate Apache and restart it.
If the old renewal dies with an ARI replaces error
The broken old renewal produced an error similar to:
Failed to create order:
Could not validate ARI 'replaces' field
Repeatedly running the bad renewal did not fix it.
Creating a fresh certificate using the steps above did.
Afterward, open:
A: Manage renewals
Select only the old errored helvete.pizza renewal and choose:
C: Cancel renewal
Do not revoke the certificate merely to remove a dead renewal definition.
Keep the healthy safecracker.helvete.pizza renewal and the new healthy helvete.pizza renewal.
Metadata troubleshooting
If an Update does not appear on Updates Home, verify:
type: update
date: YYYY-MM-DD
publish: true
If a Project does not sort based on its newest Update, verify the Project Home and Update use exactly the same project: value.
Example:
Project Home:
project: Keychron C100
Update:
project: Keychron C100
If they differ, the generator treats them as different projects.
If a note appears in Obsidian but not publicly, verify it has:
publish: true
That omission is a feature, not a bug.
Quartz troubleshooting
Homepage is a 404
Quartz expects:
content\index.md
The publisher creates it from Welcome.md.
Verify Welcome.md contains:
---
title: Welcome
publish: true
---
Then rerun the publisher.
Homepage is titled index
Same issue: make sure the title: Welcome frontmatter is present before building.
Explorer is empty and Graph View is one dot
Quartz has only received one note, usually because content was manually populated incorrectly.
Do not manually maintain ShagsLab-Web\content.
Run the publisher so it regenerates the staging directory from the vault.
@quartz-themes/default cannot be found
From:
F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web
run:
npm install @quartz-themes/default
then rebuild.
Windows PowerShell throws bizarre parse errors around normal code
The publisher must remain safe for Windows PowerShell 5.1.
The original failure came from a Unicode em dash in a UTF-8-without-BOM .ps1, which PowerShell misread and then produced a cascade of nonsense parser errors.
Keep the operational publisher script ASCII-only unless PowerShell encoding behavior is deliberately changed.
The actual backup philosophy
There are several layers here and they have different jobs:
Obsidian vault
    = original source
 
Local Git
    = local history
 
Private GitHub
    = off-machine copy + transport
 
.site\public
    = generated website snapshot
 
Web host checkout
    = deploy source
 
Apache lab folder
    = disposable live copy
The most important data is always:
F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab
If the website disappears, rebuild it.
If Apache disappears, rebuild it.
If Quartz disappears, replace it with something else.
Do not contort the vault around the website.
The website exists to present the vault.
The vault does not exist to feed the website.

Recovery scripts
The following are the working scripts used by this setup as of September 19, 2026.
Keep this guide under source control so Future Me can recreate them even if the operational copies are gone.
Publish-Lab.ps1
Save as:
F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web\Publish-Lab.ps1
param(
    [string]$VaultPath = "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab",
    [string]$QuartzRoot = "F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web",
    [string]$TrackedSiteRoot = "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab\.site\public",
    [switch]$Serve,
    [switch]$SkipGit
)
 
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
 
function Write-Step {
    param([string]$Message)
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host "==> $Message" -ForegroundColor Cyan
}
 
function Write-Utf8NoBom {
    param(
        [string]$Path,
        [string]$Text
    )
    $parent = Split-Path -Parent $Path
    if ($parent -and -not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $parent)) {
        New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $parent -Force | Out-Null
    }
    $utf8 = New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding($false)
    [System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($Path, $Text, $utf8)
}
 
function Get-RelativePathFromRoot {
    param(
        [string]$Root,
        [string]$FullPath
    )
    $rootNormalized = $Root.TrimEnd('\')
    if (-not $FullPath.StartsWith($rootNormalized, [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase)) {
        throw "Path '$FullPath' is not inside '$Root'."
    }
    return $FullPath.Substring($rootNormalized.Length).TrimStart('\')
}
 
function Get-FrontMatter {
    param([string]$Text)
 
    $result = @{}
    $normalized = $Text -replace "`r`n", "`n"
 
    if (-not $normalized.StartsWith("---`n")) {
        return $result
    }
 
    $end = $normalized.IndexOf("`n---`n", 4)
    if ($end -lt 0) {
        return $result
    }
 
    $block = $normalized.Substring(4, $end - 4)
 
    foreach ($line in ($block -split "`n")) {
        if ($line -match '^\s*([A-Za-z0-9_-]+)\s*:\s*(.*?)\s*$') {
            $key = $Matches[1].ToLowerInvariant()
            $value = $Matches[2].Trim()
 
            if (($value.StartsWith('"') -and $value.EndsWith('"')) -or
                ($value.StartsWith("'") -and $value.EndsWith("'"))) {
                $value = $value.Substring(1, $value.Length - 2)
            }
 
            $result[$key] = $value
        }
    }
 
    return $result
}
 
function Convert-ToDate {
    param([string]$Value)
 
    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($Value)) {
        return [datetime]::MinValue
    }
 
    try {
        return [datetime]::Parse($Value, [System.Globalization.CultureInfo]::InvariantCulture)
    }
    catch {
        return [datetime]::MinValue
    }
}
 
function Get-ProjectKeysFromUpdate {
    param([string]$ProjectValue)
 
    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($ProjectValue)) {
        return @()
    }
 
    # Supports the current simple format:
    # project: Keychron C100
    # project: BASS VI - Penny, GitHub
    return @(
        $ProjectValue -split ',' |
        ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } |
        Where-Object { $_ }
    )
}
 
function Get-WikiTarget {
    param([string]$RawTarget)
 
    $target = $RawTarget.Trim()
 
    if ($target.Contains('|')) {
        $target = $target.Split('|')[0]
    }
    if ($target.Contains('#')) {
        $target = $target.Split('#')[0]
    }
 
    return $target.Trim()
}
 
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $VaultPath -PathType Container)) {
    throw "Vault not found: $VaultPath"
}
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $QuartzRoot -PathType Container)) {
    throw "Quartz root not found: $QuartzRoot"
}
 
$ContentRoot = Join-Path $QuartzRoot "content"
$PublicRoot = Join-Path $QuartzRoot "public"
 
Write-Step "Scanning Shag's Lab"
 
$noteFiles = Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $VaultPath -Recurse -File -Filter "*.md" |
    Where-Object {
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.git\\' -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.obsidian\\' -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.trash\\'
    }
 
$notes = foreach ($file in $noteFiles) {
    $text = Get-Content -LiteralPath $file.FullName -Raw
    $fm = Get-FrontMatter -Text $text
 
    $publish = $false
    if ($fm.ContainsKey("publish")) {
        $publish = $fm["publish"].ToLowerInvariant() -eq "true"
    }
 
    $draft = $false
    if ($fm.ContainsKey("draft")) {
        $draft = $fm["draft"].ToLowerInvariant() -eq "true"
    }
 
    $type = if ($fm.ContainsKey("type")) { $fm["type"].ToLowerInvariant() } else { "" }
    $title = if ($fm.ContainsKey("title")) { $fm["title"] } else { $file.BaseName }
    $dateRaw = if ($fm.ContainsKey("date")) { $fm["date"] } else { "" }
    $project = if ($fm.ContainsKey("project")) { $fm["project"] } else { "" }
    $status = if ($fm.ContainsKey("status")) { $fm["status"] } else { "" }
 
    [pscustomobject]@{
        Source       = $file.FullName
        Relative     = Get-RelativePathFromRoot -Root $VaultPath -FullPath $file.FullName
        Directory    = $file.DirectoryName
        Name         = $file.BaseName
        Text         = $text
        FrontMatter  = $fm
        Publish      = ($publish -and -not $draft)
        Type         = $type
        Title        = $title
        DateRaw      = $dateRaw
        DateValue    = Convert-ToDate -Value $dateRaw
        Project      = $project
        Status       = $status
        Modified     = $file.LastWriteTime
    }
}
 
$publicUpdates = @(
    $notes |
    Where-Object { $_.Publish -and $_.Type -eq "update" } |
    Sort-Object @{ Expression = { $_.DateValue }; Descending = $true },
                @{ Expression = { $_.Name }; Descending = $true }
)
 
$publicProjects = @(
    $notes |
    Where-Object { $_.Publish -and $_.Type -eq "project" }
)
 
Write-Step "Generating Updates Home"
 
$updatesLines = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string]
$updatesLines.Add("---")
$updatesLines.Add("title: Updates Home")
$updatesLines.Add("type: index")
$updatesLines.Add("publish: true")
$updatesLines.Add("---")
$updatesLines.Add("")
$updatesLines.Add("*This page is auto-generated.*")
$updatesLines.Add("")
$updatesLines.Add("## Latest Updates")
$updatesLines.Add("")
 
foreach ($update in $publicUpdates) {
    $target = ($update.Relative -replace '\\', '/') -replace '\.md$', ''
    $updatesLines.Add("- [[$target|$($update.Name)]]")
}
 
if ($publicUpdates.Count -eq 0) {
    $updatesLines.Add("_No published updates yet._")
}
 
if ($publicUpdates.Count -gt 0) {
    $updatesLines.Add("")
    $updatesLines.Add("*Last Updated: $($publicUpdates[0].DateValue.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd'))*")
}
 
$updatesHomePath = Join-Path $VaultPath "Updates\Updates Home.md"
Write-Utf8NoBom -Path $updatesHomePath -Text (($updatesLines -join "`r`n") + "`r`n")
 
Write-Step "Generating Projects Home"
 
$projectRows = foreach ($projectNote in $publicProjects) {
    $displayName = $projectNote.Title
    if ($displayName -eq $projectNote.Name) {
        $displayName = $displayName -replace '\s+Home$', ''
    }
 
    $projectKey = if (-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($projectNote.Project)) {
        $projectNote.Project
    }
    else {
        $displayName
    }
 
    $matchingUpdates = @(
        $publicUpdates | Where-Object {
            $keys = Get-ProjectKeysFromUpdate -ProjectValue $_.Project
            $keys | Where-Object { $_ -ieq $projectKey }
        }
    )
 
    if ($matchingUpdates.Count -gt 0) {
        $activityDate = ($matchingUpdates | Sort-Object DateValue -Descending | Select-Object -First 1).DateValue
    }
    else {
        $activityDate = $projectNote.Modified
        Write-Warning "No published update matched project '$projectKey'. Using the project note's modified date. Add 'project: $projectKey' to the project Home note and use the same value on its update posts for exact sorting."
    }
 
    [pscustomobject]@{
        Note         = $projectNote
        DisplayName  = $displayName
        ProjectKey   = $projectKey
        ActivityDate = $activityDate
    }
}
 
$projectRows = @(
    $projectRows |
    Sort-Object @{ Expression = { $_.ActivityDate }; Descending = $true },
                @{ Expression = { $_.DisplayName }; Descending = $false }
)
 
$projectsLines = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string]
$projectsLines.Add("---")
$projectsLines.Add("title: Projects Home")
$projectsLines.Add("type: index")
$projectsLines.Add("publish: true")
$projectsLines.Add("---")
$projectsLines.Add("")
$projectsLines.Add("*This page is auto-generated.*")
$projectsLines.Add("")
$projectsLines.Add("## Projects")
$projectsLines.Add("")
 
foreach ($row in $projectRows) {
    $target = ($row.Note.Relative -replace '\\', '/') -replace '\.md$', ''
    $dateText = $row.ActivityDate.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd")
    $projectsLines.Add("- [[$target|$($row.DisplayName)]] - last activity $dateText")
}
 
if ($projectRows.Count -eq 0) {
    $projectsLines.Add("_No published projects yet._")
}
 
if ($projectRows.Count -gt 0) {
    $projectsLines.Add("")
    $projectsLines.Add("*Last Updated: $($projectRows[0].ActivityDate.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd'))*")
}
 
$projectsHomePath = Join-Path $VaultPath "Projects\Projects Home.md"
Write-Utf8NoBom -Path $projectsHomePath -Text (($projectsLines -join "`r`n") + "`r`n")
 
# Re-scan so the freshly generated Home pages are included.
$noteFiles = Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $VaultPath -Recurse -File -Filter "*.md" |
    Where-Object {
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.git\\' -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.obsidian\\' -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.trash\\'
    }
 
$notes = foreach ($file in $noteFiles) {
    $text = Get-Content -LiteralPath $file.FullName -Raw
    $fm = Get-FrontMatter -Text $text
 
    $publish = $false
    if ($fm.ContainsKey("publish")) {
        $publish = $fm["publish"].ToLowerInvariant() -eq "true"
    }
 
    $draft = $false
    if ($fm.ContainsKey("draft")) {
        $draft = $fm["draft"].ToLowerInvariant() -eq "true"
    }
 
    [pscustomobject]@{
        Source      = $file.FullName
        Relative    = Get-RelativePathFromRoot -Root $VaultPath -FullPath $file.FullName
        Directory   = $file.DirectoryName
        Name        = $file.BaseName
        Text        = $text
        Publish     = ($publish -and -not $draft)
    }
}
 
Write-Step "Creating clean public staging copy"
 
if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $ContentRoot) {
    Remove-Item -LiteralPath $ContentRoot -Recurse -Force
}
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $ContentRoot -Force | Out-Null
 
$publishedNotes = @($notes | Where-Object { $_.Publish })
 
$welcome = $publishedNotes | Where-Object { $_.Relative -ieq "Welcome.md" } | Select-Object -First 1
if (-not $welcome) {
    throw "Welcome.md must contain 'publish: true'. It becomes the public site's index.md."
}
 
foreach ($note in $publishedNotes) {
    if ($note.Relative -ieq "Welcome.md") {
        $destination = Join-Path $ContentRoot "index.md"
    }
    else {
        $destination = Join-Path $ContentRoot $note.Relative
    }
 
    $parent = Split-Path -Parent $destination
    if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $parent)) {
        New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $parent -Force | Out-Null
    }
 
    Copy-Item -LiteralPath $note.Source -Destination $destination -Force
}
 
# Build an index of non-Markdown files so only attachments actually referenced
# by published notes are copied into the website staging area.
$assetFiles = Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $VaultPath -Recurse -File |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Extension -ine ".md" -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.git\\' -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.obsidian\\' -and
        $_.FullName -notmatch '\\\.trash\\'
    }
 
$assetsByName = @{}
foreach ($asset in $assetFiles) {
    $key = $asset.Name.ToLowerInvariant()
    if (-not $assetsByName.ContainsKey($key)) {
        $assetsByName[$key] = New-Object System.Collections.ArrayList
    }
    [void]$assetsByName[$key].Add($asset)
}
 
function Resolve-Attachment {
    param(
        [string]$Target,
        [string]$NoteDirectory
    )
 
    $clean = Get-WikiTarget -RawTarget $Target
    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($clean)) {
        return $null
    }
 
    if ($clean -match '^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*://') {
        return $null
    }
 
    $cleanFs = $clean -replace '/', '\'
 
    $sameFolder = Join-Path $NoteDirectory $cleanFs
    if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $sameFolder -PathType Leaf) {
        $item = Get-Item -LiteralPath $sameFolder
        if ($item.Extension -ine ".md") {
            return $item
        }
    }
 
    $fromRoot = Join-Path $VaultPath $cleanFs
    if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $fromRoot -PathType Leaf) {
        $item = Get-Item -LiteralPath $fromRoot
        if ($item.Extension -ine ".md") {
            return $item
        }
    }
 
    $leaf = Split-Path -Leaf $cleanFs
    if ($assetsByName.ContainsKey($leaf.ToLowerInvariant())) {
        $matches = @($assetsByName[$leaf.ToLowerInvariant()])
        if ($matches.Count -gt 1) {
            Write-Warning "Attachment '$clean' is ambiguous; using '$($matches[0].FullName)'."
        }
        return $matches[0]
    }
 
    return $null
}
 
$copiedAssets = @{}
 
foreach ($note in $publishedNotes) {
    $targets = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string]
 
    foreach ($match in [regex]::Matches($note.Text, '\[\[([^\]]+)\]\]')) {
        $targets.Add($match.Groups[1].Value)
    }
 
    foreach ($match in [regex]::Matches($note.Text, '!?\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)]+)\)')) {
        $targets.Add($match.Groups[1].Value)
    }
 
    foreach ($target in $targets) {
        $asset = Resolve-Attachment -Target $target -NoteDirectory $note.Directory
        if (-not $asset) {
            continue
        }
 
        if ($copiedAssets.ContainsKey($asset.FullName)) {
            continue
        }
 
        $relativeAsset = Get-RelativePathFromRoot -Root $VaultPath -FullPath $asset.FullName
        $assetDestination = Join-Path $ContentRoot $relativeAsset
        $assetParent = Split-Path -Parent $assetDestination
 
        if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $assetParent)) {
            New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $assetParent -Force | Out-Null
        }
 
        Copy-Item -LiteralPath $asset.FullName -Destination $assetDestination -Force
        $copiedAssets[$asset.FullName] = $true
    }
}
 
Write-Host "Published notes: $($publishedNotes.Count)"
Write-Host "Referenced attachments copied: $($copiedAssets.Count)"
 
Write-Step "Building Quartz"
 
Push-Location -LiteralPath $QuartzRoot
try {
    if ($Serve) {
        Write-Host "Starting local preview at http://localhost:8080/"
        Write-Host "Press Ctrl+C when you're finished."
        & npx quartz build --serve
        exit $LASTEXITCODE
    }
 
    & npx quartz build
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        throw "Quartz build failed with exit code $LASTEXITCODE."
    }
}
finally {
    Pop-Location
}
 
Write-Step "Copying built website into the same Git repo"
 
$trackedParent = Split-Path -Parent $TrackedSiteRoot
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $trackedParent)) {
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $trackedParent -Force | Out-Null
}
 
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $TrackedSiteRoot)) {
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $TrackedSiteRoot -Force | Out-Null
}
 
& robocopy $PublicRoot $TrackedSiteRoot /MIR /R:2 /W:1 /NFL /NDL /NP
$robocopyExit = $LASTEXITCODE
 
if ($robocopyExit -ge 8) {
    throw "robocopy site staging failed with exit code $robocopyExit."
}
 
Write-Host "Tracked website output: $TrackedSiteRoot"
 
if (-not $SkipGit) {
    Write-Step "Backing up vault with Git"
 
    & git -C $VaultPath add -A
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        throw "git add failed."
    }
 
    $changes = & git -C $VaultPath status --porcelain
 
    if ($changes) {
        $commitMessage = "Publish Shag's Lab $(Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')"
        & git -C $VaultPath commit -m $commitMessage
        if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
            throw "git commit failed."
        }
    }
    else {
        Write-Host "Vault working tree is already clean."
    }
 
    $remotes = @(& git -C $VaultPath remote)
    if ($remotes -contains "origin") {
        & git -C $VaultPath push origin main
        if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
            throw "git push failed."
        }
        Write-Host "Pushed vault backup to origin/main."
    }
    else {
        Write-Warning "No Git remote named 'origin' exists yet. Local Git backup is complete, but nothing was pushed off-machine."
    }
}
 
Write-Step "Done"
Write-Host "Quartz build output: $PublicRoot"
Write-Host "Tracked site output: $TrackedSiteRoot"
Write-Host ""
Write-Host "On the web host, run Update-ShagsLab-WebHost.bat."

@echo off
setlocal
 
rem === Shag's Lab website updater - WEB HOST ===
rem Pulls the latest repo from GitHub, then mirrors the generated site
rem into Apache's live web root.
 
set "REPO_DIR=C:\PGN\ShagsLab"
set "WEB_DIR=C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab"
set "SITE_DIR=%REPO_DIR%\.site\public"
 
echo.
echo ========================================
echo   Updating Shag's Lab
echo ========================================
echo.
 
echo Checking Git...
where git >nul 2>&1
if errorlevel 1 (
    echo ERROR: Git is not installed or is not in PATH on this machine.
    echo.
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
 
git --version
echo.
 
if not exist "%REPO_DIR%\.git" (
    echo ERROR: Git repository not found:
    echo   %REPO_DIR%
    echo.
    echo The repo must be cloned to that folder first.
    echo.
    echo Example:
    echo   git clone YOUR_GITHUB_REPO_URL "%REPO_DIR%"
    echo.
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
 
cd /d "%REPO_DIR%"
 
echo Repository found.
echo.
echo Current remotes:
git remote -v
echo.
 
echo Pulling latest version from origin/main...
git pull --ff-only origin main
 
if errorlevel 1 (
    echo.
    echo ERROR: Git pull failed.
    echo Common causes:
    echo   - GitHub authentication is not set up on this PC
    echo   - origin is missing or points to the wrong repo
    echo   - the branch is not named main
    echo.
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
 
if not exist "%SITE_DIR%\index.html" (
    echo.
    echo ERROR: Generated site was not found:
    echo   %SITE_DIR%
    echo.
    echo Run Publish-ShagsLab-HomePC.bat on the home PC first,
    echo make sure it pushes successfully, then run this updater again.
    echo.
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
 
if not exist "%WEB_DIR%" (
    echo Creating live web folder:
    echo   %WEB_DIR%
    mkdir "%WEB_DIR%"
)
 
echo.
echo Publishing generated site to Apache...
robocopy "%SITE_DIR%" "%WEB_DIR%" /MIR /R:2 /W:1 /NFL /NDL /NP
 
if errorlevel 8 (
    echo.
    echo ERROR: Website copy failed.
    echo.
    pause
    exit /b 1
)
 
echo.
echo ========================================
echo   Shag's Lab is up to date
echo ========================================
echo.
echo Repository:
echo   %REPO_DIR%
echo.
echo Live website:
echo   %WEB_DIR%
echo.
pause
 
exit /b 0

Total disaster-recovery manual for PGN - Ewok Around and Find Out
Last verified: September 11, 2026

If you are reading this in 2036 with a blank Windows server and absolutely no memory of how any of this worked: breathe, make coffee, and follow Full restoration from scratch in order. Do not improvise the directory names.
This repository contains the custom configuration and source code for:

The GOG edition of STAR WARS Battlefront II (Classic, 2005)
SWBF2Admin/WebAdmin
The two-way Discord ↔ game chat bridge (HK-47)
The SvelteKit/Tailwind landing page and seasonal leaderboard
The PowerShell exporter used to build a safe GitHub backup

It intentionally does not contain the installed game, third-party executables, passwords, tokens, runtime logs, or the live player database.

The rule that keeps the public server alive


                  
                  CAUTION
                  
                

NEVER start, restart, administer, or even open the server desktop with Windows Remote Desktop Connection (RDC/RDP).


SWBF2Admin’s official documentation warns that GOG Galaxy communications do not work properly over Windows RDP and that components launched through RDP can disappear from the public master list. This was also reproduced on this server: the server remained public and joinable for nearly 24 hours under Chrome Remote Desktop, then stopped being reachable after an RDC session was opened.
Use one of these instead:

Chrome Remote Desktop (CRD) — current known-good method
VNC — acceptable future replacement
A physical/local console session

After using CRD, disconnect from it; do not sign out of Windows. Closing the CRD client does not stop the console session or game server. WebAdmin and the Discord bridge are safe to use after the server is running.
Official reference: SWBF2Admin — Preparing the gameserver

System architecture
flowchart TD
    Players["Battlefront players"] <--> Game["SWBFII game server"]
    Game <--> Admin["SWBF2Admin + WebAdmin"]
    Admin <--> Bridge["HK-47 Discord bridge"]
    Bridge <--> Discord["#swbfii-chat"]
    Admin --> DB["SWBF2Admin.sqlite"]
    DB --> Site["XAMPP landing page + leaderboard"]

The bridge talks only to WebAdmin on localhost. The website reads the SQLite database in read-only mode. Neither service needs direct public RCON access.

I Made A Custom Driver?!
Sorry, I just had to add some punctuation since I can’t have it in the title. So cool! Seems ridiculous but this is a bucket list item for me. Something I’ve always wanted to do.
I got a new Keychron c100 keyboard, its 10x10 keys in a perfect square. I knew I would be able to find something to do with it, but I couldn’t. I really wanted to make it have a bunch of symbols that I hardly used, because maybe I would use them more, or maybe that’s just cool?

Turns out, Keychron’s Launcher was not quite up to the job.
You can assign normal keys just fine, but there are only 16 macro slots. I tried making custom profiles and modifying the exported JSON to force functionality that just wasn’t there.
No dice.
I kept digging and, after asking the oracle, ChatGPT, I learned that the firmware Keychron was using was open source and based on QMK.
And QMK is basically an entire open-source keyboard firmware ecosystem.
Oh.
Well now we’re cooking.
The Keychron C100 8K has its own target in Keychron’s QMK fork, which meant there was nothing stopping me from compiling my own firmware for it.
Except, you know, not knowing how to do that.
So I installed the QMK toolchain in WSL, cloned Keychron’s firmware repository, installed an ARM compiler, installed dfu-util, fought with USB drivers for a little while, passed the keyboard’s DFU device through from Windows into WSL…
And eventually compiled my first firmware.
I decided not to immediately flash all 100 keys because I am not completely stupid.
The first test firmware did one thing.
The top-left key typed:
©

That was it.
Ninety-nine useless keys and one copyright symbol.
I flashed it.
Opened Notepad.
Pressed the button.
©

Holy shit.
So then I pressed it about twelve times.
©©©©©©©©©©©©

Obviously.
That proved the whole thing worked.
The trick was QMK’s Unicode support. Instead of trying to store 100 macros or relying on Keychron Launcher, every physical key could be defined directly in the firmware as a Unicode code point.
So something like this:
UC(0x00A9)

becomes:
©

No macro slot.
No copy and paste.
No Alt-code cheat sheet.
The keyboard itself knows what that key is supposed to do.
Once the test worked, I compiled the real firmware.
All 100 keys.
And somehow, against all odds, every single one worked:
©®™℠℗§¶№†‡
¢£€¥₹₩₽₺₴₿
±×÷≠≈≤≥∞√∫
∑∏∂∆πµΩλαβ
°‰¹²³⁰½¼¾⌀
…•·–—‐“”‘’
←↑→↓↔↕↖↗↘↙
⇐⇒⇑⇓↩↪↺↻⤴⤵
✓✔✕✖☑☐☒★☆※
♠♥♦♣♪♫☺☹♂♀

It’s such a stupid keyboard.
I love it.
And yes, I know.
Technically I didn’t make a driver.
I made custom firmware.
But “I Made Custom Keyboard Firmware” doesn’t have quite the same energy, and I also had to manually install a USB driver along the way, so I’m invoking the rule of cool.
More importantly, this was one of those projects where I started with absolutely no intention of learning anything particularly deep.
I just wanted a button that typed ©.
Then one limitation turned into another question.
That question turned into QMK.
QMK turned into cross-compiling ARM firmware.
That turned into DFU bootloaders, USB passthrough, flashing microcontrollers, and writing my own keyboard layout at the firmware level.
And now I own a keyboard with a dedicated ‰ key.
Worth it.
Next: I need to make labels for all 100 keycaps, because right now I have created the world’s least intuitive keyboard.

If you want to do this yourself check out Keychron C100 Custom Firmware How Do

updates/2026-09-17---i-built-a-booru-lib.content:
I Built A Booru Librarian?!
This started as an extremely normal request.
I wanted to save images from a booru. You know, for science.
Not everything. Just posts with specific copyright, character, artist, or general tags. I am a man of specific tastes, of course. I knew I could make some type of script to check the site every so often, grab anything new, and sort it into folders automatically.
You know.
A tiny librarian.
Except the library is Rule34.
The first version was pretty straightforward. I made a little Python program that talks to Rule34’s JSON API, asks for exact tags, remembers what it has already seen in a SQLite database, and downloads new matches.
Windows Task Scheduler wakes it up once an hour, it checks the shelves, and then it goes back to sleep.
Something like this:
Rule34 Tag Archive\
├── Copyright\
├── Character\
├── Artist\
└── General\
Beautiful.
Then authentication broke.
The API returned a string instead of the list I expected, my error message helpfully said the response was a str, and absolutely nobody learned anything.
After fixing that, the real message appeared:
Missing authentication.
Cool.
Once the credentials were actually credentials, the thing worked.
Then I wanted history.
The normal watcher deliberately starts small. On the first run it downloads the newest 25 posts for each tag, records the older results as a baseline, and then only watches for new stuff. That was a good safety feature, but now I wanted the whole archive.
The kind of greed they talk about in the bible.
So I added a backfill mode.
It walks through every page for every configured tag, politely waits between requests, and records its work so it can be stopped and restarted without beginning from zero.
Then I remembered general tags existed.
So those got their own section too.
At this point the machine was happily collecting files, sorting them, resuming interrupted downloads, and quietly doing its job every hour.

And then I had a tiny storage-related revelation.
I was already 500 GB in. Holy… Nico Robin you’re going to rob me of all of my terabytes.

And I had barely scratched the surface.
The original version copied a matching image into every matching folder. If one post matched a character, an artist, and two general tags, congratulations: I had just stored the exact same bytes four times.
That is not organization.
That is a very expensive confidence trick.
So I rebuilt the archive layout around NTFS hard links.
Now every post has one canonical physical file inside a hidden management folder:
.r34-watcher\files\...
The files visible under Copyright, Character, Artist, and General are hard links to that same file.
They look and behave like normal files. They open normally. They can have different paths. They can appear in five tag folders at once.
But the actual image data exists on disk once.
It is basically one book with several cards in the old library catalog.
Or, in filesystem language, several filenames pointing at the same NTFS file record.
This is extremely cool.
It also means Windows Explorer can be a little dramatic. Folder Properties may add the apparent size of every link and claim the archive is much larger than the space it really occupies. The drive’s free-space number is the one that tells the truth.
There are rules.
The whole archive has to stay on one NTFS volume because hard links cannot cross drives. The .r34-watcher folder is not junk and absolutely cannot be deleted. A normal copy to another drive can expand the links back into separate physical copies.
So the clever storage trick is also the part that requires the most respect.
We also had a brief adventure with Windows Task Scheduler.
Moving the project folder without reinstalling the task leaves Windows pointing at the old path. Running PowerShell commands in Command Prompt makes Command Prompt complain that PowerShell commands do not exist. And if a watcher process is killed at precisely the wrong moment, a little lock file can remain behind and insist another run is still happening.
Every one of those problems is fixable.
None of them feels fixable while Windows is confidently telling you the program is already running when it definitely is not.
But now the project has:

Exact Copyright, Character, Artist, and General tag lists
Authenticated API requests
An intentionally limited first run
A resumable full-history backfill
SQLite history
Automatic hourly checks through Task Scheduler
One physical copy per post, no matter how many watched folders it matches
Link repair if a managed folder entry disappears
Configuration validation
Rotating logs
A proper uninstall script
Automated tests on Windows

And, somehow, it uses nothing outside the Python standard library.
No pip install ritual.
No mysterious dependency tower.
Just Python, PowerShell, SQLite, Task Scheduler, and NTFS doing increasingly elaborate things so I do not have to right-click Save Image As.
This project began as:

Could this check a few tags for me?

It turned into API pagination, authentication, resumable state, rate limiting, filesystem identity, hard links, scheduled jobs, and a small amount of swearing at stale process locks.
Worth it.

The librarian lives!
And now it only buys one copy of each book.
Next: make the archive easier to move between drives without accidentally turning every hard link back into a full duplicate.
If you want to build it, recover it, move it, or figure out why Windows thinks it is already running, check out Rule34 Tag Watcher - Doomsday Rebuild Guide.
Or check out Rule34 Tag Watcher - How Do for the README on GitHub.
Or, go to GitHub. You’re an adult (I assume), I have faith in you to make the right decision

updates/2026-09-18.1---a-mixed-bag-sort-.content:
Some days are not about getting one larger thing done, but many smaller things that we have been putting off for awhile. Also some days we just need to be thankful we did anything at all!
Bass VI Setup

I have been meaning to setup my new Bass VI, (in antigua finish ou la laa), but that would require actually taking the old factory strings off, and replacing them with the extra fan-say La Bella strings. Flatwounds, oh yah. This should give the bass a new and different sound, so I am anxious to hear it, but also anxious of wasting 60$ on string I may just hate.
Also, there is some quirks with this style of instrument produced by Fender and Squire. The bridge can rock back and forth and putting new strings on and ensuring the tuning is correct can be difficult when setup this way. A nice little hack is to throw these brass ferrules in the bridge post holes, the inside and outside diameters are a perfect fit and the bridge should stay in tune way better.

And what do you know? It does! that was worth about 15 cents and my time. But the string? That’s another story.
You know, I don’t hate them, I also don’t think I love them. They are their own thing, they do in fact have a distinct and i would call muted sound. It sounds interesting distorted but the true beauty comes in on clean. The Bass sings, the notes are so clear and clean, this is where the world of difference is. Playing something like Hey You but Pink Floyd, the strings really do the heavy lifting for the song. I do like this tone, it’s not an all use case sort of thing, but I see the appeal. If the Bass VI was fretless, then I think this would be a no brainer… and maybe that’s an idea for the future.

I did not intonate of adjust the truss rod, the bass was playing so well and the action felt good, so i left it as is. Later I will install strap locks so the strap does never comes off accidentally and send my precious, hideous bass flying into harms way or left solely to the whims of gravity.
Oh, Penny. Why that name for a bass? Well, all instruments need a name. To me, it kind of looks like a moldy Piece of Bread? Work with me here, so Penny is short for Penicillin? Dad joke levels of bad. Go ahead, groan, I’ll wait.
One observation I had was the tuners are still shit. I don’t find them to be this bass on my other Squire Bass VI, so that’s a little disappointing. I think in the near future I will replace the tuners will better quality ones, but that is a project for another day…
GitHub Page
This one does not need an essay write up. My GitHub landing page was a little too simple and lack luster, I wanted to put more about me and infect it with my personality so I did. I have grown since I wrote that landing and most of that code in my repo, and with me starting to archive projects more religiously this seemed like a good time for it.
It’s quite possible I will change the landing a few times, and that it will be totally different in a few years time, so until then and until that update let me just post al ink to what it looks like now.
GitHub Landing 9-18-2026

updates/2026-09-18.2---i-made-my-midi-dr.filePath: Updates/2026-09-18.2 - I Made My MIDI Drummer Worse on Purpose.md
updates/2026-09-18.2---i-made-my-midi-dr.title: 2026-09-18.2 - I Made My MIDI Drummer Worse on Purpose
updates/2026-09-18.2---i-made-my-midi-dr.content:
I write a lot of my drum parts in Guitar Pro, I’m not saying it’s the best, but when you’ve used something for 25+ years and it just works it’s kind of hard to switch.
It is less great when I export the MIDI, drop it into REAPER, and discover that my drummer has apparently been replaced by a machine with atomic-clock timing and perfect control over every muscle in its body. I know metal drummers are precise but not everyone is Gene Hoglan.
Every hit is exactly where I told it to be, every note is perfectly obedient.
It sounds fake AF.
Obviously there are already ways to “humanize” MIDI. Move notes a little bit. Randomize the velocity. Make everything slightly wrong.
But that started bothering me too, because humans aren’t just random.
A drummer doesn’t have four identical sticks floating around the kit. They have two hands, two feet, a dominant side, a weaker side, and a limited number of limbs that can only be in so many places at once.
So I made a REAPER script that tries to make my fake drummer worse at drumming in a more realistic way.
The goal was pretty simple.
I wanted to export a finished drum part from Guitar Pro, bring it into REAPER, select the MIDI item, run one script, and have it come out sounding less like Guitar Pro.
Not random. Human.
The first part was figuring out what every MIDI note actually represented.
So I made a drum map:
[35] = "Kick Drum",
[38] = "Snare Drum",
[42] = "Closed Hi-Hat",
[49] = "Crash Cymbal",
[51] = "Ride Cymbal",
And so on.
Then I gave every drum piece a default limb.
[36] = "DF",  -- Dominant Foot
[38] = "DH",  -- Dominant Hand
[42] = "NDH", -- Non-Dominant Hand
[44] = "NDF", -- Non-Dominant Foot
That was the important part.
Instead of looking at a MIDI note and saying: “Move this somewhere around here.”
The script can look at it and say:
“This is a snare hit. That is probably the dominant hand.”
“This is a hi-hat. That is probably the other hand.”
“This is a kick. Foot.”
Now we’re cooking.
Once every note has a limb, the four limbs can have their own personalities.
In Configuration.lua I gave them separate strength values:
dominateHandStrength = 99
nondominateHandStrength = 91
dominateFootStrength = 93
nondominateFootStrength = 87
So the dominant hand is naturally stronger than the non-dominant hand.
The feet aren’t identical either.
Then they each get their own timing bias, plus a little random variation.
velocityRandomRange = 10
timingRandomRange = 2
That means the “humanization” isn’t just one random number being thrown at every note.
A snare hit and a hi-hat hit can drift differently because they came from different simulated limbs.
The same goes for velocity.
Which is a very complicated way of making a computer slightly worse.
Perfect.
There was another problem though.
What happens when the MIDI asks one hand to hit two things at the same time? Or three?
The script groups notes that occur together and tries to resolve limb conflicts.
If two notes both want the dominant hand, one of them can be reassigned to the non-dominant hand.
The same basic idea applies to the feet.
There is also logic for alternating limbs through sequences instead of having one imaginary arm perform an entire drum roll like a woodpecker.
That part made the whole thing feel much more interesting to me.
I wasn’t just adding noise anymore. I was starting to model a person.
A very simple person. With four limbs. Who lives inside REAPER.
The script also has a list of MIDI notes that I don’t want in a standard drum-kit part.
Things like bongos, agogos, claves, vibraslap, cowbells, metronome hits, and a bunch of other percussion are marked separately from the kit pieces I actually expect.
So while analyzing the MIDI it can flag things that don’t belong in the kind of drum track I’m trying to process.
The actual program ended up split into a few modules:
Main.lua
Init.lua
Mapping.lua
AnalyzeMidi.lua
ProcessMidi.lua
Main.lua is basically the conductor.
It initializes the script, loads the mappings, analyzes the MIDI, and then processes it.
AnalyzeMidi.lua is where the interesting drummer-brain stuff happens.
It reads the MIDI notes, assigns limbs, groups simultaneous hits, alternates limbs where appropriate, checks for conflicts, and builds an internal representation of the performance.
Then ProcessMidi.lua takes that information and actually changes the MIDI.
Velocity gets adjusted around the configured strength for the limb.
Timing gets shifted according to that limb’s bias plus some randomness.
Then the original MIDI notes are replaced with the processed ones.
And REAPER says:
Humanization Complete!
I also apparently started making a GUI for this.
But that’s a project for another day. Maybe.
The current version in the repository is 0.9, which feels appropriate because there are definitely still rough edges.
There are checks I would tighten up.
The configuration could be much friendlier.
The GUI obviously went wherever unfinished GUIs go to die.
And there is a lot more that could theoretically be modeled if I ever wanted to get ridiculous with it.
Tempo.
Fatigue.
Accents.
Ghost notes.
How far a hand has to move across the kit.
Different playing styles.
Different actual drummers.
That last one is probably the most interesting possibility.
The configuration is already structured around the idea of an emulated player’s timing and strength.
So instead of having one generic “humanize” button, there is at least the beginning of a system where different configurations could represent different feels.
Not random imperfection.
Specific imperfection.
Which I think is the thing I like most about this project.
Computers are extremely good at doing exactly what you tell them.
Music often sounds better when they don’t.
REAPER Drum Humanizer

updates/2026-09-19.1---my-mini-retro-tel.title: 2026-09-19.1 - My Mini Retro Television Channels
updates/2026-09-19.1---my-mini-retro-tel.content:
I Turned A Tiny TV Into A Cartridge Console
I bought this little thing called a My Mini Retro Television.
It is exactly what it sounds like.

A tiny fake old television with a little screen, a speaker, some buttons, and a bunch of old videos loaded onto it.
You turn it on, it plays a little startup video, and then you can click through the videos like you are changing channels.
There is even a little static / channel-change animation between videos.
It is very stupid. I love it.
The first thing I did was plug it into my computer because obviously I needed to know what was actually going on inside it.
The internal storage showed up like a normal USB drive with a few gigabytes of videos on it.
There were also a bunch of weird tiny files like:
._VIDEODROME TV SPOT.mp4
._TWILIGHT ZONE MARATHON.mp4
._TONIGHT ON HBO 1990.mp4
They were only a few KB each and looked like broken videos.
Turns out those are just AppleDouble metadata files from a Mac.
So that mystery was solved pretty quickly.
The actual videos were normal MP4 files.
One file immediately stood out:
0 MY MINI RETRO TELEVISION.mp4
That was the startup video.
I pulled it off the TV and inspected it so I would have a known-good format to work from.
It is:
H.264
618x480
30 FPS
yuv420p
AAC audio
44.1 kHz stereo
Which is incredibly useful because now I know exactly what this tiny little goblin television already likes.
So naturally the next question was:
Can I put my own videos on it?
Yes. Very yes.
I deleted the videos from the internal storage, backed everything up first because I am reckless but not stupid, and put Planet of the Apes on it. All of them. A whole galaxy of apes.
It played!
At this point I discovered something even better. The TV also supports USB flash drives.
This changed the entire project.
Instead of constantly replacing the internal storage, I could leave the TV basically stock and treat USB drives like cartridges.
Tiny TV cartridges.
I made a little diagnostic pack with four videos:
000 STARTUP SORT TEST.mp4
001 CHANNEL ONE.mp4
002 CHANNEL TWO.mp4
003 CHANNEL THREE.mp4
Each one had a giant number on screen and a different number of beeps so I could tell exactly what the TV was doing.
The first problem was immediately very 2026.
All the flash drives I could find were 64GB.
Windows will not normally let you format a 64GB drive as FAT32 through the regular format dialog.
Of course.
So I just threw the test files on it and plugged it intop the little TV anyways.
That worked perfectly. The TV saw the drive. The videos played. The audio worked. The files played sequentially. The numbering controlled the order.
Beautiful. So my problem, was not even a problem.
Then things got more interesting.
The TV behaves differently when it is playing from internal storage versus USB.
With the internal storage, I get:
startup video
video
channel-change static
video
channel-change static
...
power-off movie
With a USB drive inserted, I get:
startup video
"USB drive inserted"
USB video
USB video
USB video
...
No channel-change animation. No power-off movie.
And there is a hardware / firmware message on screen telling me the USB drive was inserted.
That message is now on my list.
I do not know if I can remove it. I do not know if I can change the text.
I definitely do not know if I can replace it with a tiny VHS cassette graphic.
But I have now ordered two more televisions as backups, so science may happen.
The USB discovery also gave me the dumbest and therefore best idea in the entire project. The flash drives should be physical media.
I bought twenty 4GB flash drives.

The idea is to make each one feel like a little cable TV cartridge.
Not twenty different shows.
Actual stations.
Things like:
NICK01
NICK02
NICK03
NICK04
SNICK
 
CN01
CN02
CN03
CN04
CN05
 
KWB01
KWB02
FOX96
BOOM01
BOOM02
 
POWER
SCIFI
UPN
HBO
AMC
So instead of putting one season of one show on a drive, I am building little fake broadcasts.
A Nickelodeon cart might have Rugrats, Hey Arnold!, CatDog, Doug, Angry Beavers, Rocko, etc.
A Cartoon Network cart might have Dexter’s Laboratory, The Powerpuff Girls, Ed, Edd n Eddy, Batman, Freakazoid, and Animaniacs.
The goal is not to make a “best of” playlist.
I want it to feel like I turned the TV on in 1999 and just started watching whatever happened to be on.
That meant I had to start researching what was actually syndicated and rerun heavily instead of just picking my favorite episodes.
Because if I am going to pretend this tiny plastic television is cable TV, apparently I am going to take that responsibility seriously.
I also dumped the contents of my TV library into a giant file list so I could start planning the carts around what I actually own.
There is a lot.
Nickelodeon.
Cartoon Network.
Kids’ WB.
Star Trek.
Voyager.
Tales from the Crypt.
Three Stooges.
Beast Wars.

It turns out I have accidentally been preparing for this project for years.
The next missing piece was commercials.
If the whole point is to make this feel like old television, then going:
Rugrats
Hey Arnold!
CatDog
Doug
is not enough.
It needs this:
Rugrats
1997 cereal commercial
Hey Arnold!
Nintendo commercial
CatDog
Pizza Hut commercial
Doug
PSA
Now we are getting somewhere.
I started looking for old commercial archives and found a few big collections.
Some have individually clipped commercials.
Some are giant VHS commercial-break dumps.
Some are old Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, Kids’ WB, Fox Kids, Disney, HBO-ish late-night stuff, and general 90s television.
I am currently downloading several of those collections.
Some of the torrents are being annoying and hanging on missing files because apparently even my fake 90s cable system has infrastructure problems.
The plan is to build a large commercial library, hopefully around 120-150 clips, then split them into pools like:
KIDS_90S
KIDS_00S
GENERAL_90S
GENERAL_00S
LATE_NIGHT
PSA
Then each fake station cartridge can pull commercials from the appropriate pool.
I am also looking for old network IDs and bumpers.
The little clips that say things like:
You're watching Nickelodeon
We'll be right back
Now back to the show
Cartoon Network
Kids' WB
Those will make the cartridges feel much more like actual TV stations instead of folders full of videos.
Eventually I want each cart to start with a station ident, play a sequence of shows, drop in commercials between them, and maybe use fake static or tracking glitches to recreate the channel-change effect that USB mode loses.
There is also going to be a cart-builder script because I am absolutely not doing all of this manually twenty times.
The builder will eventually take:
a station
a list of shows
a commercial pool
some bumpers
a startup ident
and turn all of it into correctly numbered MP4 files encoded for the tiny television.
That part is still ahead of me.
Right now I have the television figured out enough to know this is actually going to work.
The USB cartridges work.
The playback order works.
The format works.
The station lineup exists.
The commercial archives are downloading.
And there are twenty tiny flash drives on the way to becoming the world’s least useful cable provider.
I also want to 3D print little VHS cassette cases for the flash drives. Maybe. Probably.
One thing at a time.
